query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the mechanism by which it would preserve stability, the predicted outcome relative to the same nanoparticles without the intervention, relevant temperature, time, and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a thermal-exposure experiment with measurements and failure criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The single intervention of forming a core-shell structure in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can overcome the unresolved risk of structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
generation.intervention: Forming a core-shell structure in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles
generation.conditions: Operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime
generation.mechanism: The formation of a core-shell structure in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can enhance the thermal stability and prevent the growth and agglomeration of nanoparticles, thus preserving the structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles during operation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved catalytic performance and stability of the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles without a core-shell structure
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 773-1173 K, time range of several hours, and compositional range of five or more metals
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the formation of a core-shell structure in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and its effect on the structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Thermal-exposure experiment with high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with and without a core-shell structure, operated in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime for several hours
measurements: Structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a core-shell structure show no improvement in catalytic performance and stability compared to those without a core-shell structure, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The investigated Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 single-crystalline HEA is a nanostructured magnetic material, consisting of A2 nanoparticles of rather uniform size with an average diameter of 64 nm, chemical composition Co19Cr56Fe25, and about 6% volume fraction, embedded in a B2 matrix of composition Al28Co25Fe15Ni32 with about 94% volume fraction. Quite generally, the nanoparticles start showing size-specific physical properties that are different from those of a bulk material at diameters typically below about 20 nm. The A2 nanoparticle sizes in the ACCFN material are just at the boundary between a nanomaterial and a bulk material, but due to further clustering of the elements on the nm scale within the nanoparticles, they behave as true nanomagnetic objects.

Our TEM EDS elemental mapping has identified and confirmed the core-shell structure of the A2 nanoparticles. Magnetic measurements have revealed that the nanoparticle cores with composition Co-Cr-Fe order asperomagnetically, which follows the expectations due to the presence of two FM elements (Co and Fe) and one antiferromagnetic element (Cr). The nanoparticle shells are strongly enriched in the two ferromagnetic elements Co and Fe, so they are expected to be ferromagnetic. This could not be verified experimentally by the employed bulk magnetization measurement methods due to the presence of a much stronger FM signal from the B2 Al-Co-Fe-Ni matrix.
